name: Thread
seoDesc: Thread: work out basic pitch diameter from the major diameter tolerance and the minor diameter tolerance. A free construction calculator with the formula,…
summary: The Thread calculator turns the major diameter tolerance, the minor diameter tolerance and more into basic pitch diameter. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Thread calculator work?
sections.html:
The Thread calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports basic pitch diameter in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the external tolerance position); then you type in the major diameter tolerance (Td), the minor diameter tolerance (TD₁), the maximum major diameter and the minimum major diameter (Internal thread limits).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Thread calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Basic pitch diameter=-3 ÷ 8 × the square root of (3) × thread pitch + basic major diameter
Basic major diameter=(5 ÷ 8) × the square root of (3) × thread pitch + basic minor diameter
Basic pitch diameter=(1 ÷ 4) × the square root of (3) × thread pitch + basic minor diameter
Height of fundamental triangle (H)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (3) × thread pitch
Minimum root radius (Rmin)=(1 ÷ 8) × thread pitch
Pitch diameter tolerance (Td₂)=2 × the square root of (3) × minimum root radius (Rmin) × the square root of (Y × (2 × minimum root radius (Rmin) − Y) ÷ (minimum root radius (Rmin) ^ 2)) + 2 × minimum root radius (Rmin) + 2 × Y

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Calculate set to External thread dimensions, Thread pitch set to 1.0 mm, Basic major diameter = 30 mm and Basic pitch diameter = 30 mm. Working through the relationship above gives Basic minor diameter = -78.2532 mm, Height of fundamental triangle (H) = 86.6025 mm, Minimum root radius (Rmin) = 12.5 mm and Cmax = 23.087 mm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Basic minor diameter = -78.2532 mm, Height of fundamental triangle (H) = 86.6025 mm, Minimum root radius (Rmin) = 12.5 mm and Cmax = 23.087 mm should be roughly the size you expected from Calculate set to External thread dimensions and Thread pitch set to 1.0 mm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Thread calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the major diameter tolerance, the minor diameter tolerance and the maximum major diameter — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Thread calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns basic pitch diameter, derived from the major diameter tolerance, the minor diameter tolerance and the maximum major diameter. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Thread calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the major diameter tolerance, the minor diameter tolerance, the maximum major diameter and the minimum major diameter, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter basic major diameter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Basic major diameter opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (8 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Basic minor diameter = -78.2532 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Thread calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
